title: Weekly links September 18: gender inequality in India, sleep, jobs, farms, and more…
gist: A weekly links roundup: son preference and female labor norms in India, sleep economics, weak on-the-job learning in developing-country jobs, Rodrik's claim that services now outpace manufacturing in India's marginal labor productivity, and phone tutoring delivering ~4 years of instruction per $100.

insights.claim: Seema Jayachandran argues India's son preference centres on the eldest son, producing declining health inputs from older to younger brothers and subtler disadvantages for girls.
insights.speaker: @worldbank
insights.so_what: Gender norms shape human capital distribution in India's labor force.
insights.quote: the eldest son in the family is the special one

insights.claim: Bangladesh is described as the 'demonstration project' for India: workplaces engineered to fit female seclusion norms, such as work-from-home jobs, might erode those norms over time.
insights.speaker: @worldbank
insights.so_what: Remote/female-friendly job models could unlock India's low female labor participation.
insights.quote: Bangladesh is the “demonstration project” for India.
insights.locator: discussion also on low female labor force participation

insights.claim: Dani Rodrik notes the marginal product of labor in India is now higher in services than manufacturing, and argues retail increasingly provides the linkages once attributed to manufacturing.
insights.speaker: @worldbank
insights.so_what: Supports services-led growth thesis for India over manufacturing-led industrial policy.

insights.claim: Employment in low- and middle-income countries is concentrated in jobs where little learning occurs, per Joana Silva.
insights.speaker: @worldbank
insights.so_what: Weak workplace skill accumulation limits productivity growth in emerging markets.
insights.quote: employment in low- and middle-income countries is concentrated in jobs where little learning occurs.
insights.locator: On Let’s Talk Development, Joana Silva

insights.claim: A new VoxDevLit reviews why structural transformation out of agriculture is slow and why more productive farms do not grow much bigger.
insights.speaker: @worldbank
insights.so_what: Slow farm consolidation constrains agri-productivity plays in developing markets.

insights.claim: Johan Fourie highlights research that people sleep less in higher-income countries and the rich sleep less than the poor, and an RCT nudging college students to sleep more raised grades.
insights.speaker: @worldbank
insights.so_what: Sleep as a productivity input is a niche wellness/health theme.

insights.claim: Five RCTs led by Noam Angrist in India, Kenya, Nepal, the Philippines and Uganda found phone-call tutoring effective across settings, delivering about 4 years of high-quality instruction per US$100, while text messages had mixed results.
insights.speaker: @worldbank
insights.so_what: Low-cost phone tutoring is a highly scalable edtech model for emergencies and low-income markets.
insights.quote: deliver approximately 4 years of high-quality instruction per US$100 spent

insights.claim: A Science Policy Forum proposes a four-phase implementation-science framework for education linking efficacy and effectiveness trials to policy plans and practice at scale.
insights.speaker: @worldbank
insights.so_what: Frames how education interventions scale, useful in diligence on edtech scale claims.
insights.locator: And then in a Policy Forum in Science

insights.claim: David Deming and Gina Raimondo discuss designing tax incentives to push companies to invest more in workers, including career switchers.
insights.speaker: @worldbank
insights.so_what: Possible future US policy on employer training tax credits.
insights.locator: The Context Window with David Deming
